summary: A 1970 note by Steve Crocker on third-level ideas for the Network Information Center (NIC), and other miscellaneous thoughts. It was updated by RFC 80 and RFC 93 and replaced by RFC 123.

plainLanguage.summary: This note proposes how one host could connect a user to another host's logger. It also records an early agreement about the character format for network consoles.

subtitle: A 1970 note describing a proposed remote logger connection and a shared console format.

tldr.problem: Early network hosts needed a procedure for connecting a local process to a remote host's logger.
tldr.mechanism: A using host requests contact at socket 1. If accepted, the serving host returns an even 32-bit socket number, and the hosts establish connections using that number and the next one.
tldr.outcome: RFC 66 was updated by RFC 80 and RFC 93 and obsoleted by RFC 123. It also proposes a console format using 7-bit ASCII in 8-bit fields.

sections.title: The Proposed Dial-Up Procedure
sections.content:
RFC 66 records ideas discussed at a meeting with representatives from BBN and MIT. The dial-up procedure is intended to connect a process at a using site to the logger at a serving site.

The using process requests a connection from its receive socket to socket 1 on the serving host. The serving host may refuse with a standard close. If it accepts, it sends an even 32-bit number naming a receive socket; that socket and the next higher-numbered socket are reserved for contact with the user.
sections.plainLanguage: The local host asks the remote host's contact socket for service. If accepted, the remote host gives back a pair of socket numbers for the session.

sections.title: Setting Up the Logger Connections
sections.content:
After sending its socket number, the serving NCP closes the initial connection and requests the contact connections using the returned socket and its successor. The using host sets up matching connections from its own receive socket and the next socket.

Once these connections are established, the user should be connected to the serving host's logger. The RFC illustrates the process with RTS, STR, CLS, and ALL protocol messages.
sections.plainLanguage: The two hosts use the returned socket pair to establish the logger connection. The first contact connection is then closed.

sections.title: The Standard Console
sections.content:
The note records agreement on an initial network console standard: 7-bit ASCII carried in 8-bit fields with the eighth bit set, sent in contiguous streams. The specific character codes are referred to in appendix H of the IMP Operations manual.

For break or interrupt, many systems can use a standard character. A system needing another signal can send an INR message over the control link.
sections.plainLanguage: The console text uses ASCII carried in fixed-size fields. A control-link message can signal an interrupt when a standard character is not suitable.
